newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolian president runs neck and neck in polls.
newsitem.headline: Mongolian president runs neck and neck in polls.

text.p: Mongolia will hold its presidential elections on Sunday, with incumbent President Punsaknaagin Ochirbat running neck and neck against the standard-bearer of opposition former communists.
The popularity of the 55-year-old president has slipped in the run-up to the elections due to public anger at the nation's economic woes, including rising unemployment and inflation.

A public opinion poll conducted by Sant Maaral Centre, a think tank, this month showed Nstaagin Bagabandi, 47, candidate of the opposition formerly communist Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party, ahead with 51 percent support, while Ochirbat had 44 percent.

The elections, the second direct presidential elections in this sprawling land of the steppes, will not change the balance of power in the landlocked nation in north Asia. Ochirbat's Democratic Union Coalition has been in power for 10 months and dominates parliament, the Great Hural.
But if Bagabandi, a former speaker of parliament, wins he could cripple the Great Hural with his power to veto bills it passes.

The charismatic Bagabandi has campaigned to slow the pace of reforms to allow Mongolians a breather during the transition from Soviet-style central planning to a market economy that has caused widespread economic dislocation.
Bagabandi, the youngest of the three candidates, was greeted by firecrackers when he stopped by a concert on Thursday evening attended by thousands of teenage students.
"I will help Mongolian youths find jobs," he said to the cheers of the crowd. Unemployment was over 30 percent in 1994.
Ochirbat has promised to eradicate poverty and embrace democracy. One in five Mongolians lives below the official poverty line with an income of about $10 a month.
"We will keep what there is to keep and throw out what there is to throw out...and (adopt) a market economy," Ochirbat told hundreds of university students in the capital on Thursday.

In Mongolia's first direct presidential elections in June 1993, Ochirbat won 57.8 percent of the vote. He ran as a candidate for the then-opposition Democrats after being dumped by the then-ruling Mongolian People's Revoloutionary Party.
The Democrats won a stunning 50 of the 76 seats in parliament in elections last June to take power after 75 years of rule by Mongolia's communists and their heirs.
About 1.2 million of Mongolia's 2.3 million people were eligible to go to the polls on Sunday. Results were expected to be known on Monday at the earliest.
A third presidential candidate, Jambin Gombojav, 56, a member of parliament, is running on a Mongolian Traditional United Party ticket.
